stimulus
  1. ACh / CCK bind basolateral M3 and CCK1 receptors (human CCK evidence is mixed)
  2. Gq → phospholipase C → IP₃ made at the cell base
  3. IP₃ opens IP₃ receptors on the ER: Ca²⁺ is released, first at the apical pole, then as a wave
  4. Ca²⁺ drives granule fusion with the apical membrane (exocytosis)
  5. Release into the lumen: inactive proenzymes (e.g. trypsinogen) and active amylase and lipase

active enzyme (amylase, lipase) inactive proenzyme (e.g. trypsinogen) Ca²⁺ IP₃ ACh CCK

Hover or focus a part for a short explanation. Raise the stimulus: receptors fire, Ca²⁺ rises at the apex and spreads, granules fuse and empty into the lumen.

Sources

Educational only, not medical advice. On a phone, swipe the figure sideways and tap a part to read about it. Schematic, not to scale: positions, counts and speeds are illustrative and the levels come from a qualitative model, not measurements. No measured number is shown.

  • Cell polarity, granules, receptors, nerves. Nucleus and rough ER basal, Golgi above, zymogen granules apical, apical secretion, acetylcholine and CCK as stimuli: Pandol SJ, The Exocrine Pancreas, Morgan & Claypool 2010 (NCBI Bookshelf NBK54128).
  • Secretory pathway. Rough ER to condensing vacuoles of the Golgi complex, which become zymogen granules: Jamieson and Palade, Intracellular transport of secretory proteins in the pancreatic exocrine cell. II. Transport to condensing vacuoles and zymogen granules, J Cell Biol 1967 (guinea pig). ER-to-Golgi transport in COPII-coated vesicles: Barlowe and Miller, Genetics 2013 (general review, largely yeast).
  • Signalling. Gq, PLC, IP₃ and DAG, and Ca²⁺-triggered exocytosis: Williams, Annu Rev Physiol 2001. Local Ca²⁺ spikes in the secretory pole: Thorn et al., Cell 1993 (mouse). IP₃ receptors densest at the apical pole, store refilling across the basal membrane: Petersen, Cell Calcium 2003. Basal muscarinic receptors drive apical Ca²⁺ signals at a distance: Ashby et al., J Biol Chem 2003. Perigranular mitochondria confine local Ca²⁺ signals: Tinel et al., EMBO J 1999 (mouse). SNAREs in granule exocytosis: Pickett et al., Biochem Biophys Res Commun 2007. Harm from sustained high Ca²⁺: Raraty et al., PNAS 2000.
  • CCK in humans. Ji et al., Gastroenterology 2001; Murphy et al., Gastroenterology 2008.
  • Active versus inactive enzymes. Fieker et al., Clin Exp Gastroenterol 2011 (full text: lipases and amylase are secreted in active form, proteases as proenzymes); review of human pancreatic enzymes: Whitcomb and Lowe, Dig Dis Sci 2007.
  • Binucleate cells and duct start. Some acinar cells have two nuclei and the duct system begins with centroacinar cells; both are general histology, shown in words only.
  • Duct fluid. Lee et al., Physiol Rev 2012.

Note. Amylase and lipase are secreted in active form; only the proteases (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase) are secreted as proenzymes, so the figure labels the release that way.

Simplified. The lumen is a narrow schematic channel and fluid flow is not drawn. One granule-release site per granule is shown, and granules are replaced instantly. Receptor, G protein and PLC symbols are generic: one muscarinic and one CCK receptor per side, with no receptor numbers or subtype details beyond M3 and CCK1. Omitted: a second nucleus, mitochondria (including the perigranular belt that confines the apical Ca²⁺ signal), centroacinar cells at the start of the duct, neighbouring acinar cells, the actin web under the apical membrane, compound exocytosis, store-operated Ca²⁺ entry channels, Ca²⁺ pumps, DAG signalling, and other receptors (for example secretin and VIP).
